title: Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids
gist: Security researchers Vangelis Stykas and Felipe Solferini showed at Black Hat that tens of millions of GPS trackers and children's smartwatches sold under dozens of Western consumer brands run on just three Shenzhen-based backend platforms — YiQingTeng/SETracker, NewGPS2012 and SinoTrack — all carrying flaws as basic as missing authentication and SQL injection. They live-demonstrated the risk by tracking a WIRED reporter across New York, silently taking photos from his sub-$30 watch and eavesdropping on his office audio; most vendors had ignored months of disclosure warnings.

themes.theme: Three Shenzhen backends behind tens of millions of trackers

insights.claim: An audit of more than 70 GPS-enabled watches and car accessories found that tens of millions of GPS tracker gadgets sold worldwide originate from just three Shenzhen-based supply chains: YiQingTeng (also branded Wonlex / Shenzhen 3G Electronics, app SETracker), NewGPS2012, and SinoTrack.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Consumer-IoT risk in the tracker category is concentrated in three private Chinese platform vendors, not in the hundreds of retail brands — a single backend failure is a category-wide event for any retailer or insurer exposed to these SKUs.
insights.quote: tens of millions of GPS tracker gadgets came from just three supply chains
insights.locator: Combined with another major GPS platform known as SinoTrack

insights.claim: Of more than 70 geolocation devices analyzed, over 30 run on YiQingTeng's technology and backend servers and another 30-plus car and child trackers run on the separate Shenzhen platform NewGPS2012.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete concentration ratio for due diligence: roughly 90% of tested devices map to two platforms, so brand-level vendor screening is nearly worthless without backend attribution.
insights.locator: At the Black Hat cybersecurity conference today

insights.claim: All three dominant GPS tracker platforms were found to have significant security flaws, in some cases as simple as a total lack of authentication that allowed anyone to access any device.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: These are not sophisticated exploit chains but baseline control failures, implying remediation requires re-architecting the platforms rather than patching — a long tail of unfixed exposure.
insights.locator: All three, the researchers found in their analysis

insights.claim: The apparent diversity of GPS tracking device brands is an illusion: differently branded watches sold in different European countries route children's location data to the same myaqsh.com backend hosted on Alibaba Cloud in mainland China.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Brand-level risk models systematically understate correlated exposure in white-labeled hardware; the right unit of analysis is the backend operator, not the label on the box.
insights.quote: A parent in Sweden buying a ‘SafeKid’ watch and a parent in Spain buying a ‘SaveFamily’ watch are both sending their child's location data to the same vulnerable myaqsh.com backend on Alibaba Cloud in mainland China, without knowing it
insights.locator: they write in a whitepaper shared with WIRED

insights.claim: In the white-label hardware model a single backend vulnerability simultaneously compromises dozens of consumer brands, and consumers have no mechanism to determine which backend their product actually uses.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Creates an information asymmetry that no amount of consumer diligence can close — an argument for regulatory backend disclosure requirements and a recurring liability theme for retailers stocking these devices.
insights.quote: consumers have no way to tell which backend their product uses
insights.locator: The white-label model means a vulnerability in one backend

insights.claim: The sheer number of brands and models of cheap GPS devices has made identifying the genuinely insecure gadgets nearly impossible for consumers, which is why the researchers framed their Black Hat work around supply-chain attribution rather than individual bugs.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Signals where security research value is migrating: mapping concentration and provenance beats enumerating CVEs when the market is fragmented at the surface and concentrated underneath.
insights.locator: More than any specific vulnerability

insights.claim: A researcher tracked a WIRED reporter's exact location on a Brooklyn block using only Wi-Fi network identifiers transmitted by a child's smartwatch to a remote server, even while the watch's GPS feature was malfunctioning.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Disabling or losing GPS does not neutralize these devices — Wi-Fi SSID beaconing is a redundant, largely unmonitored location channel that survives the obvious mitigation.
insights.locator: In fact, Stykas had been monitoring the reporter’s location

insights.claim: The hijacked smartwatch let researchers silently take camera photos of the wearer in an elevator and at his desk, and stream microphone audio to a third party, with no indication on the device that it was being used to spy.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: These devices function as fully capable covert surveillance implants inside homes and offices — a corporate counter-espionage exposure, not just a child-safety one.
insights.quote: At no point did the watch show any sign that it was listening, taking photos, or otherwise being hacked.
insights.locator: When the reporter arrived at WIRED’s Manhattan headquarters

insights.claim: Targeting a specific SETracker-based device required nothing more than the parent's registered email address, and an authentication flaw would have allowed anyone to send commands to any device on the platform.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: The attack cost per victim is effectively zero and targeting is trivial, which is what turns a technical bug into a mass-exploitation scenario.
insights.locator: In the case of YiQingTeng, the manufacturer of the watch

insights.claim: Attackers can also enumerate compromised devices in bulk and then search them for the ones physically nearest to them or matching a target's identifying information, inverting the usual targeting problem.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Enables opportunistic, proximity-based stalking at scale — the threat model relevant to predators and to physical-security teams, not only to targeted espionage.
insights.locator: Stykas says he could have easily targeted devices in other ways

insights.claim: The demonstrated exploit set on children's watches includes location tracking, location disabling and spoofing, interception and spoofing of text and audio messages, replacement of the emergency contacts a parent configured, silent audio eavesdropping, and photo and video capture.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: The emergency-contact replacement capability converts a safety device into an active abduction-facilitation tool, which is the detail most likely to trigger regulatory action.
insights.locator: leaving children’s watches vulnerable to tracking by a hacker

insights.claim: The researcher characterizes the exposure as catastrophic and limited only by an attacker's imagination, arguing millions of children sit behind low-hanging-fruit vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Sets the rhetorical frame likely to drive post-Black Hat press cycles and regulator attention toward cheap imported IoT.
insights.quote: Your criminal mind is the only limitation in exploiting those devices.
insights.locator: Millions of kids are being exposed and vulnerable

insights.claim: For GPS-enabled car accessories the researchers could track device locations and spoof messages that could potentially unlock or disable vehicles, though they stopped short of testing on real cars.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Extends the blast radius from privacy harm to physical vehicle control — relevant to fleet operators and auto insurers who mandate aftermarket telematics dongles.
insights.locator: For some GPS-enabled car accessories

insights.claim: A demonstration account on SinoTrack could be used to send commands to any of the platform's millions of devices, and a SQL injection flaw exposed tens of thousands of devices' locations, passwords and vehicle records.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A leftover demo credential granting platform-wide command authority is the kind of governance failure that supports negligence claims and import restrictions.
insights.locator: In the case of SinoTrack, the researchers say they found

insights.claim: On NewGPS2012 the researchers achieved remote code execution on company servers and found evidence of a prior compromise, suggesting unauthorized parties may already have had access to the tracking backend for an unknown period.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Moves this from theoretical risk to probable in-the-wild exploitation, and means historical location data on tens of thousands of users should be assumed already leaked.
insights.locator: Finally, for NewGPS2012 devices

themes.theme: Disclosure failure and a decade of ignored warnings

insights.claim: SETracker's representative told WIRED the reported issues 'have been resolved long before' even as researchers were actively hacking a SETracker watch that same week, and the platform's fixes only appeared hours before the Black Hat talk.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Public disclosure deadlines, not private responsible disclosure, are what actually produce patches in this segment — a pattern worth pricing into any IoT vendor remediation timeline.
insights.quote: the issues you mentioned have been resolved long before
insights.locator: When WIRED reached a representative of SETracker

insights.claim: SinoTrack and NewGPS2012 did not respond to WIRED's requests for comment and the researchers' hacking techniques against those systems still appeared to work as of publication.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Two of the three dominant platforms remain live, unpatched attack surfaces after public disclosure — an ongoing exposure rather than a resolved incident.
insights.locator: Sinotrack and the NewGPS2012 platform didn’t respond

insights.claim: This is at least the fourth documented wave of warnings about hackable GPS trackers, following Stykas and Michael Gruhn's 2018 Trackmageddon research, Pen Test Partners and Norwegian government warnings in 2017-2018, and a 2020 Münster University study that found serious flaws in five of six children's smartwatches tested.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Nearly a decade of disclosure has produced no durable improvement, evidence that reputational pressure alone does not fix commodity hardware supply chains — the case for mandated standards.
insights.locator: Children’s GPS-enabled watches have also been shown

insights.claim: The researcher's own expectation of a redemption narrative failed: after months of notification, many vendors simply ignored the warnings and the flaws still worked when retested on a newly purchased watch.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Assume no remediation by default for sub-$30 imported connected devices; the economics of a $30 watch do not support a security function at all.
insights.quote: I really hoped we could tell a nice story that there were vulnerabilities and they fixed them. But in many cases, they didn’t,
insights.locator: Yet somehow, Stykas says, people keep putting cheap

insights.claim: The specific watch used in the demonstration cost less than $30, was sold by an obscure brand called CJC and manufactured by YiQingTeng Electronics in Shenzhen, illustrating how little the retail brand reveals about the actual maker.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Marketplace listings for these devices carry essentially no attributable accountability chain, a compliance gap for the e-commerce platforms distributing them.
insights.locator: The watch’s insecurity and the spying it enabled
